facts.value: Egyptology and Coptology
The subject of study in Egyptology and Coptology is the knowledge of the culture of Pharaonic and Christian Egypt in all its facets.
From the period of the merging of various Neolithic cultures of the northern Nile Valley in the 4th millennium BCE to the Christian-Coptic period.
Territory of the present-day Arab Republic of Egypt and the northern part of the Republic of Sudan.
The period after the Arab conquest of Egypt (640/41 CE) is covered by Oriental Studies and Semitic Studies.
Egyptology is notable for its breadth, as it traces and gradually uncovers the entire societal system of one of humanity's earliest civilizations over more than four millennia.
The subject offers many interesting connections for the modern world with its increasingly complex intercultural relations.
Egyptology increasingly links numerous seemingly divergent cultural and natural science disciplines into an optimal overall concept.
Skills in conducting archaeological fieldwork using state-of-the-art techniques.
Skills in deciphering and understanding one of the oldest writing and language systems.
Skills in art historical assessment and evaluation of the self-expressions of early human civilization.
Development of a comprehensive historical perspective through the evaluation of written and archaeological documents.
Research skills regarding one of the earliest religious systems that had an impact on Christianity, Judaism, and Islam.
Uncovering the intercultural relationships between Egypt and its neighbors in West Asia and Africa.
Reconstruction of the multifaceted history of the landscape of a cultural region shaped over millennia.

Integration of natural science disciplines (archaeometric auxiliary sciences), such as geology and petrology, geophysics, anthropology, and various biological sub-disciplines, including modern DNA analysis and palaeozoology.
The degree program imparts humanities and cultural sciences competence.
Key qualifications are taught to ensure employability even outside the main subject.
The program includes practical exercises in rhetoric.
The program includes training in didactics.
The program includes training in academic writing.
The program develops foreign language competence.
The program develops the ability to give public presentations.
Career prospects within the subject area are limited.
Employment opportunities exist in museums.
Employment opportunities exist at universities.
Employment opportunities exist in field archaeology.
Students are advised to start career orientation from the first semesters and treat it as an ongoing project throughout their studies.
A variety of tips for career orientation are provided to guide students step by step throughout their studies, or selectively according to relevance and usefulness.
Students are led to conduct their own research activities at a very early stage (e.g., when preparing presentations) due to the significant lack of textbook knowledge.
From the beginning of the studies, the ability and willingness to work independently is required.
Since courses can only cover certain aspects of a subject area or question, students are forced to acquire much of the knowledge themselves.
A high degree of commitment, willingness to perform, and perseverance is required.
Good, at least passive, knowledge of both English and French is absolutely necessary for the study of Egyptology, as a large part of the specialist literature is only available in these languages.
